title: Fibre-generic localization: scalar comparison, flatness and closed fibre
statement: Let $R\to B$ be a flat homomorphism of commutative rings [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map], and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Put $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$, $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak pA$, $C=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}B$ and $F=B\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, with localization and residue field as in [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-module-localization, def-weil-residue-field]. Assume $F$ is a nonzero integral domain. Define $\mathfrak q=\ker(B\to F)$ and $T=B\setminus\mathfrak q$. Then $\mathfrak q$ is prime and contracts to $\mathfrak p$. The ring $D=B_{\mathfrak q}$ has its canonical $A$-algebra structure and the map $B\to D$ factors through $u:C\to D$. For every $A$-module $L$ there is a natural $A$-linear isomorphism $$T^{-1}(L\otimes_R B)\xrightarrow{\sim}L\otimes_A D,\qquad (l\otimes b)/t\longmapsto l\otimes(b/t),$$ where tensor products are as in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] and the $B$-module structure on $L\otimes_RB$ is on the second factor. The $A$-module $D$ is flat. Let $\overline T\subset F$ be the multiplicative image of $T$. Every element of $\overline T$ is nonzero, and there is a canonical isomorphism $$\theta:D/\mathfrak mD\xrightarrow{\sim}\overline T^{-1}F,\qquad [b/t]\longmapsto\overline b/\overline t.$$ Under $C/\mathfrak mC\cong F$, the composite of the reduction of $u$ with $\theta$ is precisely the localization map $F\to\overline T^{-1}F$. In particular the reduction $C/\mathfrak mC\to D/\mathfrak mD$ is injective.

source.place: Tag 0810, lemma-helper-blowup-affine-space, final proof paragraph: construction and closed-fibre verification of the base-localized map into the fibre-generic localization (the elementary algebra underlying that local inclusion).

proof.text: Write $f:R\to B$ and $S=R\setminus\mathfrak p$. The fibre-ring quotient comparison identifies $F$ with $C/\mathfrak mC$ as a $B$-algebra, sending $b\otimes\overline{r/s}$ to $[f(r)b/f(s)]$. The structural map $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to F$ is injective: a nonzero element in its kernel would have an inverse, forcing $1_F=0$, contrary to the nonzero-domain hypothesis. Thus $r\in R$ maps to zero in $F$ exactly when its image in $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is zero, equivalently $r\in\mathfrak p$. For the last equivalence, $r/1\in\mathfrak pA$ implies $sr\in\mathfrak p$ for some $s\notin\mathfrak p$ by the fraction equality criterion, hence $r\in\mathfrak p$; the converse is immediate. The kernel $\mathfrak q$ is proper, and $bb'\in\mathfrak q$ implies $\bar b\bar b'=0$ in the domain $F$, hence $b\in\mathfrak q$ or $b'\in\mathfrak q$. This proves primality and $f^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$.

source.place: Tag 00E6, remark-fundamental-diagram; kernel and fraction arguments expanded from the definitions.

proof.text: Since $f(S)\subseteq T$, its elements become units in $D=T^{-1}B$. The localization universal property gives the unique map $A\to D$, $r/s\mapsto f(r)/f(s)$, and the unique map $u:C\to D$, $b/f(s)\mapsto b/f(s)$, both extending the original maps. They agree on $R$ and therefore on $A$ by uniqueness; hence $u$ is an $A$-algebra map. Apply clause (2) of localization-of-localization to $B$, its multiplicative subsets $f(S)\subseteq T$, and these maps: $u$ is a localization of $C$ at the image $U$ of $T$ under $B\to C$.

source.place: Tag 00CP, proposition-universal-property-localization, and iterating that universal property for nested multiplicative subsets.

proof.text: Regard the given $A$-module $L$ as an $R$-module. Apply the prime-localized module base-change comparison to $f:R\to B$, $M=L$, and the primes $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q$ of step 1. Its first comparison is a $D$-linear isomorphism $T^{-1}(L\otimes_RB)\to L_{\mathfrak p}\otimes_AD$, with $(l\otimes b)/t\mapsto(l/1)\otimes(b/t)$. Identify $L_{\mathfrak p}$ with $L$ by $l/s\mapsto (s/1)^{-1}l$, with inverse $l\mapsto l/1$. This is well defined: an equality of fractions is witnessed by $v(s'l-sl')=0$, and $v,s,s'$ act invertibly on $L$; it therefore gives $s^{-1}l=(s')^{-1}l'$. The two composites are identities by the fraction relation, and the map is $A$-linear by the fraction formulas for addition and scalar multiplication. Tensoring this identification and its inverse with $D$ gives inverse maps on pure tensors. Their composite with the cited comparison is the required $A$-linear isomorphism with the stated formula. For an $A$-linear map $h:L\to L'$, both routes in its naturality square send $(l\otimes b)/t$ to $h(l)\otimes(b/t)$. Every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors and every localized tensor has one denominator, so these tests prove equality on the whole module.

source.place: Tag 00DK, lemma-tensor-localization, and Tag 00SI, lemma-lci-field-change-local, displayed tensor comparison; scalar and naturality formulas expanded.

proof.text: The localization-flatness lemma makes $B\to D$ flat. Composition with the assumed flat map $R\to B$ makes $R\to D$ flat. The $A$-action of step 2 restricts to precisely this $R$-action. The flat-over-localization equivalence for $R\to A=S^{-1}R$ and the $A$-module $D$ now gives flatness of $D$ over $A$.

source.place: Tag 00HT, lemma-flat-localization, clauses (1) and (2), with composition of flat ring maps.

proof.text: Put $I=\mathfrak mC$. The ideal $ID$ is $\mathfrak mD$: both are generated in $D$ by the images of the elements of $\mathfrak m$. The quotient base-change lemma for $C\to D$ gives $D/\mathfrak mD\cong D\otimes_C(C/I)$, $[d]\mapsto d\otimes1$. Step 1 identifies $C/I$ with $F$ as a $C$-algebra. Exchange tensor factors by $d\otimes z\mapsto z\otimes d$ (its inverse is the same exchange; both respect the tensor relations and multiplication). This gives $D/\mathfrak mD\cong F\otimes_CD$. Step 2 and localization base change make $F\to F\otimes_CD$ a localization at the image of $U$ in $F$, which is exactly $\overline T$. The localization universal property identifies it uniquely with $\overline T^{-1}F$. The resulting isomorphism $\theta$ has $[b/t]\mapsto\bar b/\bar t$: in the tensor ring $1\otimes(b/t)=(\bar b\otimes1)(\bar t\otimes1)^{-1}$, because the images of $b/1,t/1\in C$ agree on the two tensor factors. This checks the formula for every fraction.
